blocks.x: Robot fleets with safety cases: autonomy bounded by signed envelopes, incident-ready telemetry on every platform, utilization measured honestly including blocked time — and dock congestion engineered away instead of normalized.
Autonomy is granted by the safety case, not the sales brochure

A robot fleet is staffed with machines: shift scheduling, task allocation, charging logistics, and the safety case that says what each robot may do unattended. The engineering spans fleet orchestration, mission autonomy with bounded loops, and the telemetry that reconstructs any incident frame by frame.

The discipline borrows from aviation: pre-flight checks, briefed missions, reported deviations, and a no-blame debrief that updates the fleet's playbooks. Utilization is measured honestly — busy, blocked, charging, down — because a robot stuck at a dock is not utilization, it is an incident signal.
Below: the failure modes that make robot fleets unsafe or theatrical, the reference architecture of bounded autonomy, and the console that keeps utilization honest.
Four failure modes that make robot fleets unsafe or theatrical
Every one of these shows up as an incident, a utilization number nobody believes, or both — the countermeasures bound autonomy by evidence and measure the fleet as it actually runs.

blocks.x: Reference architecture — bounded autonomy with incident readiness

Autonomy levels are signed per zone and task with envelope monitors enforcing them in real time, telemetry is incident-ready by design, fleet orchestration manages dock and corridor contention, and integration friction with WMS and PLCs is a scoped contract — not a surprise.

blocks.title: Reference architecture — robot fleet orchestration
blocks.note: The safety case defines the autonomy envelope per robot class; violations are telemetry events, and the envelope only widens through the debrief process with evidence.

blocks.x: One mission, assignment to envelope-checked completion

From mission assignment through path planning, envelope checks, the dock and corridor contention and completion — including the violation path and what the fleet does when a platform breaches its envelope.

blocks.title: Fleet ops loop — brief, execute, report, debrief, adjust
blocks.note: Debriefs widen envelopes only with evidence: a deviation that ended safely still updates the playbook before the envelope grows.

blocks.x: The fleet console — honest utilization as the headline
Busy utilization, blocked time and envelope violations — the three numbers that run the fleet, with blocked time reported beside busy time because flattery is how fleets hide their real capacity.

nodes.label: WMS / MES
nodes.detail: Task sources with priority semantics and timeout contracts — the fleet manager plans, the WMS decides, the boundary is explicit.

nodes.label: Fleet manager
nodes.detail: Task allocation, traffic rules and charging strategy — the distributed-systems brain with mission failure semantics defined.

nodes.label: Infrastructure control
nodes.detail: Elevators, doors, chargers — the unglamorous integrations that stall fleets; each carries timing budgets and failure fallbacks.

nodes.label: AMR robots
nodes.detail: Per-robot health contracts (battery, sensors, localization quality) with automatic mission reassignment on degradation.

nodes.label: Line controls
nodes.detail: Interlocks and handoff timing with the line PLCs — robot speed regimes tied to zone state, changes gated by safety review.

nodes.label: Safety system
nodes.detail: Safety-rated scanning with zone geometry per speed regime, TS 15066 limits for collaborative zones — the safety case is versioned with every layout change.

nodes.label: Exception desk
nodes.detail: Blocked aisles, dead robots, failed missions escalate to humans with context — the MTTR here is the trust metric.

widgets.note: Click nodes for the contract each layer carries. The safety lane overrides everything — zone geometry is versioned with layout changes, no exceptions.

Safety-case governance overlay

The safety case is a living document: envelope expansions require evidence from clean telemetry hours, incidents feed the case as findings, and the signed autonomy level per zone is visible on the floor — not buried in a vendor folder.

items: Autonomy never exceeds the safety case

blocks.x: Incident telemetry is designed before the first deployment: every platform streams the signals an investigation will ask for — because incident blindness is discovered during the incident, which is the worst possible discovery context.
Ask who signed the autonomy level for your busiest robot zone — and when it was last re-validated. The diagnostic will wire envelope monitors and honest utilization before the fleet grows.
